About Me

Who I am and what drives my work.

I'm Jinta, a sophomore studying Mechanical Engineering at UW Tacoma. I've always been fascinated by tech, and imagining somebody building it from scratch is so impressive and mind-blowing to me. That's what got me into engineering.

I was always fascinated by the possibilities that space shows us as humans, so I always dreamed about becoming an astronaut. As I grew up, that turned into an interest in the structure of rockets, jets, and robots. The idea of them finding something we don't know and changing what humanity can do forever seems really cool to me. Right now, my biggest interests are sending rockets and making robots and airplanes, which is why I'm most interested in aerospace-related engineering.

I also like finding out how math and science connect to real things. Physics 2 got me interested in electromagnetism, which led to my magnetic car project, and my music background led my partner and me to use differential equations to understand guitar frets.

I lived in Okinawa, Japan, until I was 10, so I speak both English and Japanese. Okinawa has its own culture mixed with Japanese culture, and even its own language, Uchinaguchi, which plays a big role in expressing who we are as Okinawans. We also celebrate Obon differently, with a tradition called Eisaa.

I played trumpet from 5th grade to 12th grade in jazz band, symphonic band, and marching band. I've had solos, and at solo and ensemble we got the highest score possible. As a school, we also won many marching tournaments.

Outside of school, I work part-time at Oki Golf, and a friend and I started our own local home and lawn care business. In high school, I was the captain of the golf and tennis teams, and I received the Principal's Award for Outstanding Male Student.

Outside of class, I enjoy sports like volleyball, golf, tennis, and pickleball, and I love training in the gym just as much. I also love going out with my friends and finding a side quest we can do for the day.

Project 01 · Hardware

Custom PC Build

Solo project · Built Summer 2025 · Documented through disassembly and reassembly

Project Description

For this project, I built my own PC. The goal was a PC that could handle gaming and run CAD for school, with a budget of about $1,300.

My Role

This was a solo project. I picked out the parts, built it, and tested it myself. For this portfolio, I took parts of the PC out to take photos and explain what each part does.

My Process

  • Set requirements: before picking any parts, I set what the PC needed to do: gaming at my monitor's 165 Hz, and running CAD smoothly.
  • Selected parts: I used PCPartPicker to pick out my parts and check compatibility, and I found some recommended parts from YouTube videos.
  • Assembled and tested: the build itself was pretty easy. I followed YouTube videos on building a PC and copied each step onto my PC. The challenging part was the wiring: to make it look neat, I needed to use velcro for cable management.
  • Troubleshooting: when I first turned it on, it failed, so I had to check the wires and the power supply to get everything to start. I also had to learn which cable goes to which motherboard pins. Later, I added a Scythe RGB fan whose lights work, but the fan itself doesn't spin. I'm still troubleshooting this.
  • Documented: I took out parts like the SSDs, GPU, and RAM to take photos of them, then put everything back together.
ComponentBrand / ModelKey SpecsWhy I Chose It
CPUIntel Core Ultra 5 225F10 cores (6 performance + 4 efficiency), up to 4.9 GHz, no built-in graphicsIt was around $200, and it's enough to handle most games and the CAD I will run
CPU CoolerDeepCool AS500Air cooler, single tower, 140 mm fan$50, good reviews, and easy to install
GPUGigabyte GeForce RTX 5060 (dual-fan)8 GB GDDR7 VRAMEspecially good for getting high fps and resolution in video games
RAMT-Force Vulcan DDR5 (2 × 8 GB)16 GB total, 2 sticks of DDR5 at 6000 MT/sMore affordable, and it makes running CAD easier and faster
SSDCrucial P2 (1 TB) + T-Force Z4-series (1 TB)2 TB total. Both are M.2 2280 NVMe drives: Crucial P2 is PCIe Gen3, T-Force is faster PCIe Gen4 with a graphene heat spreaderJust for extra storage
Power SupplySeasonic FOCUS GX-650650 W, 80 Plus Gold, fully modularEfficient and reliable, has enough watts for future projects I could do with the PC, and makes it easy to clean up the wires
MotherboardGigabyte B860 DS3HB860 chipset, LGA 1851 socket for Intel Core Ultra CPUs, DDR5, 8+1+2+2 phase VRMCompatible with all of my parts and fit the goal of this PC build
ToolsScrewdriver, thermal paste, phone (for following build videos), Windows installer USB drive, PCPartPicker (planning), Cinebench 2026 (stress testing)

My Solution

The final PC has an Intel Core Ultra 5 225F, a Gigabyte RTX 5060, 16 GB of DDR5 RAM, and 2 TB of storage. All of the parts I bought came to around $1,450, so I went a little over budget because of tech prices. But the FPS tests and the crash test tell me this PC is more than enough for what I will use it for. One fan still needs fixing, but everything else is working.

My Impact

I set success metrics at the start and tested the PC against them:

StabilityNo system crashes, tested with a Cinebench 2026 CPU stress test · Met: the computer never crashed. The CPU scored about 40% of the newest Intel Core Ultra 9, which may sound low, but it definitely meets the needs for my gaming and CAD, and it beats the AMD Ryzen 5 7500X3D. It placed 8th overall in Cinebench's ranking.
GPU benchmarkCinebench 2026 GPU test: got 3rd in the ranking with a score of 4,473, and it outperformed the AMD Radeon Pro W6600, a workstation GPU.
GamingFortnite on max settings at 165 fps to match my 165 Hz monitor · Nearly met: on max settings the average was 150 fps, which is close to the 165 fps max my monitor can run. On normal settings, it runs in the high 200s.
CADRuns my magnetic car model, my largest CAD file, smoothly · In progress: the car model is still being designed, so this will be tested once it is finished.

What I learned: I learned what each PC part does, the technical words, and troubleshooting. When I first turned it on, it failed, so I had to check the wires and the power supply, and I learned which cable goes to which motherboard pins.

Project 02 · Mathematical Modeling

Modeling Guitar Fret Spacing with Differential Equations

Team project with Julian Preston · Differential Equations (207) · March 2026

Project Description

A guitar changes notes using frets: each fret shortens the vibrating part of the string and raises the pitch by one semitone. The goal of this project was to use differential equations to explain how fret position, string length, and frequency are related, and why the frets on a guitar are not evenly spaced. We chose this topic because we both come from a music background from high school, and we wanted to see how differential equations can help us understand how the ratio, the frequency, and the distance between frets are connected to the math.

My Role

This was a two-person project with my partner, Julian Preston, and we went through it together. I did 70% of the writing and Julian did 70% of the math. Then we each fixed about 30% of each other's work, teaching each other and fixing each other's mistakes.

My Process

  • Research: studied how string instruments produce sound, including harmonics and how the string vibrates, using sources such as Encyclopaedia Britannica and the American Journal of Physics.
  • Semitone model: in equal-tempered tuning, each semitone multiplies the frequency by the same ratio, 21/12. We wrote this as a recursive equation, f(x+1) = 21/12·f(x), solved it to f(x) = C·(21/12)x, and derived the differential equation df/dx = ln(21/12)·C·ex·ln(21/12), where C is the open-string frequency and x is the number of frets.
  • String length model: used Mersenne's law, f = (k/L)·√(F/μ), which relates a string's frequency to its length L, tension F, and mass per length μ. Treating k, F, and μ as constants, we differentiated with respect to length to get df/dL = −k·√(F/μ)·L−2.
  • Graphing: plotted both models in Desmos to see how frequency changes across frets and string lengths.
  • Tools: Desmos, academic and reference sources for research

My Solution

We ended up with two functions. Function (1) can be used as a tool to find the difference in frequency at each fret, compared with the open string. Function (2) can be used to design the distance between one fret and the next, and it also explains why the distance between frets is not linear: getting a change in frequency on a longer string is harder than on a shorter string, so the frets near the head of the guitar are farther apart.

My Impact

Success metricWe got around an A- on the final paper, and the feedback was great.

What I would improve: The feedback said our research could have used more sources and a better understanding of other factors, like the string material.

What I learned: I learned many things from this project. One is to not be scared of all the numbers and symbols that come your way, because when you put them together piece by piece, you can find what each one means. And in the end, if you are successful, you will be able to create a solution or an equation that equals the answer. I also learned many ways that music is connected to math and science. By understanding frequency and the music notes themselves, we can figure out why certain chords and sounds are pleasing to us, and why some sound like waves crashing into each other.

Project 03 · Design & Fabrication

Magnetic-Powered 3D-Printed Car

Solo project · In progress (Fall 2026) · CAD, 3D printing, electromagnetism

Project Description

I got interested in electromagnetism through Physics 2, and I was wondering how it could be used in my own project. The goal is to design and 3D print a small toy car that moves using a battery and magnets instead of a motor, on a track made from a 6 in × 18 in sheet of 0.025 in aluminum. The main problem I expect is my beginner skill in CAD and figuring out how to model a toy car. I also want to make it so I can put a LEGO character in it.

Learning CAD

I took a CAD learning course in Onshape, Introduction to Sketching, and got a certificate of completion in November 2026. I put 15 hours into the course. Most of it was through videos they provided, which make you go through each step of what you should do to make the part. I practiced making a lot of random machine parts, like the three below. Through this, I learned that Onshape is like Google Docs for engineers.

My Role

This is a solo project. I am responsible for the full design process: the concept, the CAD model, 3D printing, assembly, and testing.

My Process

  • Concept: the ends of the battery are magnetic, so I can connect neodymium magnets to them. The track is aluminum, so the circuit is made through the magnets and the track, and this should create a thrust forward (the magnetic force on a current, F = IL × B, from Physics 2).
  • Power source: chose an AA battery over an AAA.

My Solution

This project is still in progress. The final car, its results, and what I learned will be added once it is built and tested.
